nameStory: The Tidewater Mojarra gets its name from its preference for tidal waters where fresh and salt water mix. 'Mojarra' comes from Spanish, originally used for various silvery fish in tropical waters - and this little fish certainly lives up to that silvery reputation!
description: The Tidewater Mojarra is a small, compressed silvery fish that looks like a miniature dinner plate swimming on its side. These tropical visitors rarely exceed 4-5 inches in length and have a distinctly flattened, deep body that shimmers in the water. They're occasional warm-water wanderers that sometimes drift north into New England's coastal waters during the warmest months.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely compressed and deep-bodied, like a silver coin standing on edge - you can feel how thin they are if you gently hold one between your fingers

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, highly protrusible mouth that can extend outward like a tube when feeding - watch for this unique 'kissing' feeding behavior

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant silver sides that reflect light like a mirror, with a slightly darker olive or gray back and pale belly

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Clear to slightly yellowish fins with the dorsal fin having both spiny and soft portions, feeling sharp to the touch on the front spines

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish, typically 2-4 inches in New England waters, easily fitting in the palm of your hand

habitat: In New England, Tidewater Mojarras are found in shallow coastal waters, particularly around salt marshes, tidal creeks, and protected bays with sandy or muddy bottoms. They prefer areas where freshwater streams meet the ocean, seeking out the brackish mixing zones that provide rich feeding opportunities.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters as they haven't yet migrated north from warmer southern waters.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to spot them in New England during the warmest months, usually in shallow tidal areas during high tide.
seasonality.fall: May still be present in early fall if water temperatures remain warm, but will disappear as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having returned to warmer southern coastal areas or perished in cooling waters.

funFact: Tidewater Mojarras can completely turn their mouths inside-out like a trumpet to suck small prey from crevices and sand - it's like watching a fish play a tiny invisible tuba!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young butterfish or small silversides, but the mojarra's extremely compressed, coin-like body shape and protrusible mouth make it unique. Remember: if it looks like a swimming silver dollar with lips that pop out, it's probably a mojarra!
contextualKnowledge: These fish are at the very northern edge of their range in New England and represent climate refugees - their presence often indicates unusually warm water conditions. Most New Englanders will never see one, making any sighting quite special.
compareHints: Since this is the only mojarra species regularly found in New England waters, compare it to the butterfish family - mojarras are much more compressed (flatter side-to-side) and have the distinctive protrusible mouth that butterfish lack. Young scup are also silvery and compressed, but have a more robust build and lack the tube-like feeding mouth.
